title: The Divinity of the Son in Prophecy
english: "Creator" and "Ruler" and "His peace has no limit" and "Savior" and "Christ is all in all" and "Blessed forever," and that "great is the mystery of godliness," are clear; for among the Christians, Christ is praised as an unbegotten God, and that by his own divinity "he acquires the people," because he has consubstantiality with the Father.

Thus, the saints who are now to be remembered by us speak concerning these things, to whom God, according to Psalm 19, "made known the ways of life." David, in Psalm 67, prays: "Arise, O Lord my God, by command, which I have decreed, and let a gathering of peoples surround you, and return to the heights on account of this."

One perceives, as the prophet sees, that he knows the Lord and God, and he petitions him, saying "Arise" upon your unutterable becoming-human, in the manner which you foretold: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19).

For on account of this, they say, of which salvation is surrounding us: "The nations shall surround you by faith; and you, from whence you came, shall return unseparatedly"; and in Psalm 45: "Great God, Lord, and great King over all the earth." And in Psalm 44: "From the risings of the sun even to the settings, the splendor of his beauty is from Zion; God shall come visibly"; and in Psalm 67: "Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered," and "Make way for him who has set foot toward the west; Lord is his name"; and in Psalm 69: "Arise, O God, judge the earth."

Behold, how each word lifts up the glory concerning him and suffices to persuade that he exists as the essence of the Father's unity; and that the great writer calls God he who was placed in the tomb not without life, so that he might save both the living and those departed from human affairs, and he prophesies rising, judging those who have thought wisely regarding so much and such a great blessing.
Know, however, that "the west" refers to the last times; for in them this spectacle has visibly appeared to this world.

And in Psalm 69: "In the holy is your way. Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who does wonders alone." Here the incarnate God-Word is praised without words, he who entered into the Jewish temple and taught and worked wonders.

Regarding the root: 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; great God, Lord, and appeared to us' (Ps 2:2). 27.12 If it is logical according to the prophet that the Lord who appeared to us is 'great God' and 'blessed' (that is, glorified), and also 'great King' and 'only wonder-worker,' and is the Son—it is not logical according to the heretics to imply he is lesser than his own Father. 27.13 For it is not possible for the same [person] to possess [these things] first according to the prophecy, and second according to them.

27.14 If indeed we ask of the same Psalmist, we shall learn that just as the Father is known, so also the Son exists as the God of the forefathers. 27.15 For in the 44th Psalm he has cried out: 'God has reigned over the nations. God sits upon His holy throne; rulers of peoples have been gathered with the God of Abraham' (Ps 47:8). 27.16 But they were gathered together with the God who became man, concerning whom it is sung in the 2nd Psalm: 'Why did the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against His Christ' (Ps 2:2).

27.17 But Isaiah cries out to Him without comparison as the God the Father: 'From eternity we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God besides You' (Isa 64:4). 27.18 For we saw no other God than the one born according to the saving incarnation from the Virgin Mary, nor did we hear [of any] except the one attested by God the Father: 27.19 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17).

27.20 And again, as was foretold: 'A child was born to us, a Son was given, whose rule is upon His shoulder; and His name is called Mighty God, Ruler, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come' (Isa 9:6). 27.21 He leads further with other things: 'And of His peace there is no limit.'

27.22 The Son, he says, having become man, was born as a child and was given to us, bearing upon His own shoulder the rule of this His downward birth, that is to say: He himself being the rule, having been born of a virgin and from her unspeakably having been made flesh, not granting the rule of a man's union. 27.23 And His name is: 'Mighty God, Ruler.' 27.24 He did not say 'one who has authority,' but revealed His nature, His power, His sovereignty. 27.25 Knowing this name, David sings: 'Let them know that Your name...'

title: The Fullness of Deity and the Economy of Salvation
english: Lord: 'you alone are most high over all the earth' (Psalm 53:6), saying 'alone' because of the one divinity. He called him Father of eternity, being the creator of even the past ages, because he was known by men much more through the temporal aspect of the economy.

Therefore, he called him Father, as a creator and not of uncreated nature; for one is the Father of the uncreated and consubstantial Son. And to demonstrate his divinity, he said something simple: 'there is no limit to his peace.'

And Jeremiah, or rather, for the book of Baruch is one of both, solemnly speaks about him: 'This is our God; no other shall be reckoned against him (Isaiah 42:8). He found every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his child and to Israel, the one beloved by him; after these things he appeared upon the earth and walked among men.'

If, therefore, it is not conceived in a God-befitting manner that the present scripture was spoken thus because of the shared divinity of both the unutterable hypostases, it remains to say, effectively blaspheming, that the one who created is God and Father, but not our God, and is not comparable to his Son.

Thus, the word of those who slander has fallen away and spread, making the God the Word smaller and a subordinate. For how could another be incomparable to God, 'to whom no other shall be reckoned against him'?

And again: 'gods, who did not make heaven and earth, destroyed upon the earth; Lord, who made the heavens in wisdom, he is the living and true God' (Psalm 95:3), as if there were another divinity that is not true, except that of the genuine Son of God, through whom and from whom and by whom the heavens were also provided for the whole world.

And Paul, the preeminent of men, following the same sequence, gives words fittingly concerning him, writing to Titus: 'awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, to redeem us from all lawlessness and to cleanse for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works' (Titus 2:13).

For through the being called 'the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ,' it is made manifest that he does not have a second-rank status in essence, and [the distinction] of the unoriginate toward the great God the Father.

For according to appearances it is possible to conclude that if the Son is small, how will the Father be great? If the Word God 'was when he was not' (John 1:1), he was when the name of the Father did not exist. Let it be gracious to us that we dare to say such things because of the ignorance of others. 'For piety is a beautiful habit', they say, 'for those using it'.

But through the saying 'of the one giving himself for us, in order that he might cleanse for himself a people of his own possession' (Hebrews 5:9)—not for another in order that he might cleanse a people—it follows what has been mentioned. For it signifies that he himself, the one single, self-possessing and good deity, who is the cause of all, has been determined. For it is a peculiar thing for a creator, indeed, not to surpass his own creation, if it must be said so of his own work; but for the deity of a beloved Son, having no difference from the Father, to acquire the people for himself.

And this great and true interpreter leads the argument to demonstrate that he is at once a philanthropic Savior God, and at once, as he himself veiled himself and did not show himself as superior in deity, to become with us as one of us, through a change and through sin, he asserts: 'When indeed the kindness and the philanthropy of our Savior God appeared, not because of the works which we ourselves did, but according to his great mercy, he saved us through the bath of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit'.

And he also reproaches the Colossians and makes a disparagement of the primary theology concerning him by the writings, as it has already been said in the chapter 'on the consubstantial': 'Why according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ Jesus? For in him dwells all the fullness of deity bodily' (Colossians 2:9), that is, essentially. For he also is by nature a fullness, the Father's deity existing in essence.

For 'being equal to God was not considered a robbery' (Philippians 2:6); but we received from the fullness because of his goodness. Which we by nature as slaves did not have, John saying: 'And from his fullness we all have received, and grace for grace' (John 1:16), that is, the grace of the rebirth instead of the grace which we were cast away from, striking at the first law given upon the single stock. title: The Manifestation of the Son's Divinity
english: He says, 'you are under law, but under grace' (Rom 6:14); and again, 'because in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell and through him to reconcile all things to himself' (Col 1:19-20).

These things follow the previous ones. For the Father being in the Son and the Son in the Father by nature, just as every relative is inseparable as he becomes of his own kin, even if he is divided by subsistence, the argument on the moving ground is good, even if not very deeply, but not to all clearly: 'through him and to him to reconcile all things' (Col 1:20), as it is fitting to harmonize the Son with that which was said concerning the Father: 'from whom all things' (Rom 5:17), if what has been said now and then is held soundly; 'in whom dwells all the fullness of deity' (Col 2:9).

And having written to Timothy, he theologized about him to the end, and from both sets of words he taught that the Father is not according to deity by nature. For he said such as this: 'unquestionably great is the mystery of piety: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory' (1 Tim 3:16).

For this creator and benefactor of all things was not yet clearly manifest to all, when he became willing through the salvation of all and as one of all. Therefore, 'was justified in the spirit,' that is, he was shown or confirmed even by those who had ignored him in later time to be a true God; and this, he says, is not without reason, but by that movement of our soul, as common custom has it to say: 'he who was thus justified was truly the Son of this one,' providing a proof of lineage; and at other times: 'he who was thus justified ruled well.'

And so that the argument might appear more convincing, it is said he was deemed worthy even of angels, to whom, because of his divine infinity and unseeability, he was invisible before that time, similarly to the 'only invisible God,' and to be hymned by them: 'glory to God in the highest and on earth peace, in men goodwill' (Luke 2:14); and it has been preached in all this and believed, that he who shone out unceasingly from the unspeakable light, and through philanthropy was ineffably begotten from the eternally virgin in later times, expressing all the Fatherly things in himself, has ascended.
